name: Porcelain crowns

lead: A porcelain crown is a custom-made ceramic cap that fits over a prepared tooth, restoring its shape and covering its visible surface. Because ceramic can imitate the color and translucency of enamel, crowns are widely used on front teeth that are discolored, worn, broken or misshapen.

For appearance, a crown replaces the tooth's visible surface in one piece, so color, size and outline come from the dental ceramist rather than the original tooth. Dental reviews list crowns among options for discolored teeth, alongside bleaching, microabrasion and veneers.

paras: Treatment is carried out by a dentist in several steps: assessment, shaping the tooth, a temporary crown, an impression (conventional or digital), and fitting and cementing the finished crown. The crown is made outside the mouth, often by CAD/CAM milling or firing porcelain.

Shaping the tooth is irreversible and can affect the pulp. Ceramics are brittle and can chip or fracture, and veneering porcelain on zirconia often chips. Some materials can look grey over dark teeth. Choice of material depends on the tooth position and the dentist's assessment.

angle.text: The crown replaces the visible tooth surface, so color, shape and size are set by the restoration. People use crowns on discolored, broken or misshapen front teeth.

lead: A porcelain crown, also called an all-ceramic or ceramic-veneered crown, is a tooth-colored restoration that caps an entire tooth. Dentists use it when a tooth is badly discolored, broken, worn or heavily filled, and when the goal is a natural-looking front tooth [1][2].

Its use in appearance is straightforward: the visible surface of the tooth is replaced with ceramic matched to neighboring teeth in color and translucency. Dental ceramics are chosen for crowns 'primarily for their aesthetic properties' compared with all-metal restorations, according to Wikipedia, which also describes metal-ceramic (porcelain-fused-to-metal) and all-ceramic options [1]. A 2008 review of discolored teeth lists porcelain crowns among treatments that range from bleaching and microabrasion to composite and porcelain veneers [2].
Research includes randomized trials of full-porcelain crowns and shade-matching, and Cochrane reviews comparing crowns with fillings for root-filled teeth [3][4][5].
infobox: Feldspathic/leucite ceramic, lithium disilicate, alumina, zirconia; metal-ceramic

paras: All-ceramic crowns use silica-based (feldspathic or leucite-reinforced), alumina, zirconia or lithium disilicate materials. Silica-based ceramics look the most natural but are weaker and are often layered over stronger cores; monolithic zirconia is strong but less translucent, so it is more often used on back teeth. Metal-ceramic crowns bond porcelain to a metal framework [1].
Ceramic crowns need room for material: Wikipedia cites about 2.0 mm of reduction on the biting surface and at least 1.2 mm on the sides [1].

The dentist assesses the tooth and gums, prepares the tooth, places a temporary crown, takes an impression, and fits and cements the final crown, with follow-up checks [1]. Soft-tissue contouring around the gumline is sometimes discussed as part of the aesthetic outcome in the periodontal literature [6].

Reviews of maxillary anterior crowns discuss the ingredients of optimal aesthetics [7], and a randomized clinical trial used color measurements as quality criteria for shade matching of porcelain crowns [8]. Glazing and finishing affect how porcelain looks and feels [9].

Wikipedia reports that more than 95% of CAD/CAM ceramic restorations of two block types were still successful at five years and at least 90% at ten years [1]. Ceramics are brittle, veneering porcelain on zirconia often chips, lithium disilicate can look grey over discolored teeth, and preparation can irreversibly damage the pulp [1].

A randomized trial reported short-term results of IPS-Empress full-porcelain crowns [4]. Cochrane reviews (2012, 2015) examined crowns versus conventional fillings for root-filled teeth and concluded that the comparative clinical performance was unknown or unclear because of limited trial evidence [3][5]. A randomized trial also assessed the bonding of all-porcelain crowns [10].
